INDUSTRIAL AND ENGINEERING CHEMISTRY
The theoretical fuel consumption of an ideal apparatus is
405,000 B. t. u. per barrel.
The writer believes that an effi-
ciency of 50 to 60 per cent should be attainable in practice
by use of special rotary kilns, and this would correspond to a
fuel consumption of 674,000 to 810,000 B. t. u. per barrel.
In Figure 9 are assembled three curves showing the output
or fuel economy characteristics of three types of rotary kilns
which are furnished with regenerative coolers that utilize the
secondary air to abstract 100,000 B. t. u. per barrel from the
hot clinker.
A comparison of curves 2 and 1 shows the ad-
vantage of increasing the length of the kiln while keeping the
diameter inside the brickwork constant.
The longer kiln
shows a better fuel economy at all outputs and the fuel econ-
omy is less affected by output than is the case with the shorter
kiln.
Curve 3 shows the curve for a special type of rotary
kiln, proposed by the writer, in which devices are installed
for improving heat transfer between the incoming raw mix and
the outgoing gases in the upper 40 feet of the kiln.
It is not
the purpose at this time to describe the mechanical features of
this improved type of kiln, but merely to call attention to the
possibilities for greater fuel economy which result from effi-
Vol. 21, No. 4
cient countercurrent heat transfer between gas and raw mix
in the upper end of the kiln.
Figure 10 shows curves for a kiln of 8.5 feet inside diameter
in its principal length by 240 feet long, and for the same kiln
equipped with the special devices for improving countercur-
rent heat transfer in the upper end of the kiln proposed by the
writer.
These curves again bring out the fact that in the
usual types of kilns of given length the 6-foot kiln has a better
fuel economy than the 8,5-foot kiln; but the latter has a much
greater output.
The final fact which interests the engineer is
actual commercial economy, and it is quite possible that under
usual conditions the 8.5 by 240 foot kiln will be more economi-
cal in a commercial sense than a 6 by 240 foot kiln.
This is
a problem involving all commercial factors, including cost of
fuel, labor, power, money, and the respective investments per
barrel per day of output-
Such a study must pertain only to
each special case, and is out of place here.
The special de-
vice will give substantially the same fuel economy to the
8.5 by 240 foot kiln as to the 6 by 240 foot kiln, but the rela-
tive burden put upon these devices is greater in the former
than the latter.

II—Dimethyl Ether1
Ralph L. Brown and A. E. Galloway
Pittsburgh
Experiment Station, U. S. Bureau op Mines, Pittsburgh, Pa.

RECENT report2 pre-
sented a general com-
parison of the conver-
sion into methanol of carbon
monoxide and hydrogen un-
der pressure by zinc oxide and
the basic and normal zinc
chromates.
At 400° C. and
under the conditions of the

chromate was found to be the
most active.
Work on this
catalyst has been extended to other temperatures, and a
closer inquiry has been made into the liquid products ob-
tained.
The results constitute the material of this paper.
Production of Methanol and Methyl Ether
Employing the apparatus and procedure previously de-
scribed,2 the hourly production of methanol at temperatures
between 300° and 400° C. and at 180 atmospheres average
reactant pressure was determined for space velocities of 3000
and 7500.
The initial gas contained on an average of 32+ per
cent carbon monoxide and about twice that amount of hydro-
gen.
The catalyst was prepared as previously described,2 and
the amount used was 250 cc. (248 grams).
The results are
given in Table I.
. In Figure 1 the data from columns 2 and 5 of Table I have
been plotted on the figure (No. 10) employed in the earlier
paper2 to show the three values at 400° C. and a curve
of
estimated yields obtained by the Nernst approximation for-
mula used empirically.
The new data give experimental con-
version curves for space velocities of 3000 and 7500.
It is
evident from these curves that the conversions, at low space

An important

Evidences of Formation of
Dimethyl Ether
In seeking, during the early stages of the work on methanol,
a possible reason for some of the divergence between the con-
versions demanded by the calculated equilibrium constants of
Kelley5 and those obtained experimentally by the writers at
400° C., the possibility of side reactions and their by-products
was considered.
The tendency to dehydrate as well as to dehydrogenate al-
cohols is shown by many metallic oxides, and the fact that
these properties overlap (coexist) is well known.
Many of
the oxides have been classified by Sabatier4 according to these
two tendencies into a dehydrating, dehydrogenating, and a
mixed group, which is by far the largest of the three; at the
dehydrating end of the mixed group is placed chromic oxide,
and the last member of the group of mixed behavior next to
the dehydrogenating group is zinc oxide.
The question might
be raised as to whether under certain conditions there is really
more than the one group—the mixed group.
Although rigid
application of decomposition data to synthetic prediction is
to be avoided, the reverse of the dehydrogenating influence is
utilized in the synthesis of methanol with the aid of pressure,
and it is evident that the dehydration of the methanol formed

was presented.

In addition to these theoretical considerations, there were
several indirect evidences of ether formation.
One was
the
apparently large amount of gas set free by the methanol
when it was drawn from the receiver under pressure into a
receiver at room
temperature and
1 atmosphere.
Another
was the character of the distillation curves
showing the purity
of the synthetic methanol,
as given in the earlier paper.2
In those samples produced at 400° C. there was, in addition to
a higher percentage of water, a corresponding increase in the
amount of the crude methanol, which distilled slightly under
the true boiling point of methanol.
In the same
samples
the loss in volume due to distillation was likewise indicative
of a volatile constituent.
A further indication was the fact
that in the carbon monoxide balances there was
an apparent

Examination of Methyl Ether
In addition to the foregoing evidences experimental data
were
sought.
The first test showed that the amounts of
methanol vapors and methyl ether being lost in the residual
Figure 2—Apparatus Used in Examination
of Methyl Ether
gas under the usual procedure were
negligible.
Provision
was then made to examine more
closely the gases released
when the methanol at 0° C. or below was delivered from the
pressure receiver to a flask for weighing.
These gases were
sampled after being passed through a collecting tube cooled
to —80° C., and then through concentrated sulfuric acid.
In the tube a liquid was condensed, which proved to be largely
dimethyl ether.
This liquid on fractionation gave a small
amount of residue, methanol, and a relatively large portion of a
liquid which was condensed in a tube contain-
ing metallic sodium to remove
any methanol
or water that still might remain in it.
It was
then distilled and passed into sulfuric acid at
0° C., in which it was very largely absorbed.
The unabsorbed gas would neither burn nor
support combustion.
It
was principally car-
bon dioxide and contained a little air from the
system of glass.
The ether that was collected in sulfuric acid
had the characteristic odor and the proper
boiling point of dimethyl ether.
It was
a gas
at room
temperatures, was free from unsatu-
rated hydrocarbons (before the sulfuric acid
absorption), and boiled at —23.5° C., which
excluded
the
presence
of
any
appreciable
amount
of saturated
hydrocarbons.
Its
solubility in cold sulfuric acid5 (over 400 per
cent by liquid volume at 0° C.) and almost
complete release on addition of water is char-
acteristic.8
The identification was concluded
by determining the relation of the volume
of the gas under standard conditions to its liquid volume,
and from that result calculating its molecular weight, den-
sity, and other properties.
The perfect conformance of these
characteristics with those of dimethyl ether fixed its identity
fully.

Extent of Ether Production in Methanol Synthesis
The data on the dimethyl ether produced between 300° and
400° C. as a by-product of the methanol synthesis (with nor-
mal zinc chromate as the catalyst) are given in Table I.
This
production of ether calculated
as
carbon monoxide
con-
verted to ether is shown graphically by the lower curve
in
Figure 1.
The extent to which this ether formation affects the values
for percentage conversions of carbon monoxide to methanol
in Table I is not very great.
Under the experimental condi-
tions employed, the formation of ether is slow compared with
the methanol reaction, and if the carbon monoxide converted
ultimately to ether is subtracted from the carbon monoxide
which enters the catalyst chamber, the correction is about
+0.6 per cent for the conversions in runs
F and H and negli-
gible in the others.
The influence of time of contact is evident from the data
of Table I for 350° C.
At space velocities of 3000 and 7500
the ether found was, respectively, 1.42 and 0.71 grams per
pass.
Similarly, at 375° C. the production
was
3.16 and
1.47 grams for the same respective space velocities.
Petroleum Wash-Oil Thickening in the Scrubbing
of Coke-Oven Gas1
 .
M. Ullmann, D. S. Chamberlin, C. W. Simmons, and .
A. Thorpe
Lehigh
University,
Bethlehem, Pa.
A
HIGH-BOILING petroleum oil is used in the counter-
current absorption of light oils from coke-oven gas in
scrubbing towers.
With continued use the wash oil
increases in gravity from 0.834 to 0.90 and contains a suspen-
sion which, when settled out, does not materially affect the
gravity of the oil.
This process is called thickening.
With
thickening, a wash oil reduces in absorption capacity and the
accumulation of the suspended material presents mechanical
difficulties throughout the entire system.
It is the object of
this investigation to determine the primary
cause
of such
thickening.
Cause of Thickening
Kiemstedt2 in 1925 summarized the suggested
causes
of
thickening as follows:
(1)
The oxygen content
of the gases and its influence on the
wash oil, especially on the phenols of the wash oils.
(2)
The oxidation
of hydrogen sulfide
to
sulfur and its
asphalt-forming property.
(3)
The capacity of oils for inorganic materials, especially
compounds of iron and their catalytic influence on the process.
(4)
The moisture content
of the oils.
(5)
Cracking.
(6)
The prevailing pressure
on the system.
In 1926 Hilgenstock3 pointed out that “even at this late date
no satisfactory explanation has been given for thickening.”
Offe,4 and Kattwinkel,5 although disagreeing
as to the
mechanism of thickening, point to hydrogen sulfide as the
primary cause.
Offe states that the thickening is caused by

Kattwinkel, however, views the thickening as due to polym-
erization of the wash oil by sulfuric and sulfo acids formed
from the oxidation of the hydrogen sulfide present.
Since
hydrogen sulfide is present in the coke-oven gas to the extent
of 500 grains per 100 cubic feet, such reasons
seem
quite
logical.
In addition, the wash oil on thickening increases in
sulfur content from 0.182 to 0.967 per cent.
All attempts to thicken a new
wash oil with hydrogen sul-
fide were unsuccessful. No thickening resulted when hydrogen
sulfide was bubbled through cold or hot oil for 3 weeks, or when
a saturated solution of the gas in the oil was subjected to a
treatment similar to that given in the stripping stills and heat
exchangers.
Even when steel wool was
used as
a catalyst
and the above processes duplicated, there was
no thickening.
In some
cases, however, there was
a slight and insignificant
increase in the sulfur content of the wash oil after treatment.
Another suggested mechanism is that thickening may be
the result of sulfur as such, being produced in the system by
the reduction of hydrogen sulfide.
If
was
found, however,
that flowers of sulfur, although dissolving in hot oil, would
precipitate on cooling and produce no thickening.
It has been suggested that thickening may be produced by
cracking of the wash oil in the stripping process.
Experi-
ments with new
wash oil, benzolized wash oil, and wash oil
saturated with hydrogen sulfide and flowers of sulfur, all
produce no thickening when heated to a cracking temperature.
In every case
a black, carbonaceous residue is precipitated
and the light fractions formed volatilize, but the residual oil
does not increase in gravity.
According to Bergbau and Lothringen6 the thickening may
be due to oxygen or carbon dioxide, or both, since their method
